claims.text: Controlled thermomechanical processing can concurrently improve yield strength and ductility in a conventional alloy.
Cold working followed by intermediate-temperature annealing can induce a heterogeneous bimodal grain structure.
The initial conventionally processed alloy has a homogeneous, equiaxed grain structure.
Cold working followed by annealing is a thermomechanical processing route used for alloys.
An intermediate annealing temperature, controlled cooling rate, and controlled strain rate are required for the proposed treatment.
Optimizing temperature, strain rate, and cooling rate induces partial recrystallization.
Partial recrystallization produces a mixture of fine and coarse grains.
Avoiding excessive grain growth is necessary to retain the desired bimodal grain distribution.
Fine grains increase strength through increased grain-boundary area and grain-boundary strengthening.
Coarse grains enhance ductility by permitting greater strain accommodation.
A heterogeneous microstructure containing fine and coarse grains synergistically supports strength and plasticity.
The proposed treatment will produce higher yield strength than the homogeneous-grained baseline.
The proposed treatment will produce higher ultimate tensile strength than the homogeneous-grained baseline.
The proposed treatment will produce significantly improved ductility relative to the homogeneous-grained baseline.
Conventional thermomechanical processing of the baseline alloy produces a uniform grain-size distribution.
The proposed improvement is primarily applicable to alloys amenable to grain refinement and recovery.
Alloys lacking a processing window for formation of a controlled bimodal grain distribution may not show concurrent strength and ductility improvement.
The magnitude of strength and ductility improvement depends on alloy composition and processing-parameter optimization.
